newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia defence minister at ease on NATO, funding.
newsitem.headline: Russia defence minister at ease on NATO, funding.

text.p: Defence Minister Igor Rodionov extended an olive branch to NATO on Tuesday, saying he was convinced the western defence alliance no longer posed a threat to Russia.

In conciliatory mood, he also toned down his rhetoric on the acute problems in the Russian military -- including a cash shortage and delayed reforms -- which he previously said could have catastrophic consequences for the country.
In a briefing for journalists after meeting visiting British Defence Minister Michael Portillo, Rodionov was asked whether Portillo had persuaded him NATO was no threat.

"I am convinced. But now I have to convince millions of people, above all in Russia, and we have to work on this. Just as we have to convince the West that Russia poses no threat to the West," Rodionov said.

Portillo, who arrived on Tuesday for a two-day visit to Moscow, said both sides must work to persuade people that Russia and the West were no longer enemies. "We must each work on our public attitudes at home," he said.

Russia has vigorously opposed NATO plans to expand to the east to take in some of Moscow's former East Bloc allies, but has recently softened its stance in a tacit recognition that it can do little to stop the expansion.
Rodionov, who last week raised the alarm about the parlous state of the armed forces, told Tuesday's briefing the situation had eased.
"I wouldn't call the situation in the Russian armed forces a crisis. There are certain complications and difficulties which we, especially the government, are overcoming," he said.
"The situation a month ago was more difficult, but we have overcome it and today things are improving, including funding."
A week ago Rodionov told a meeting of military top brass that Russia faced a catastrophe unless it took extreme measures to reform the army.
"The armed forces today have come to the point where a further reduction in their combat readiness could lead to unforeseable, tragic consequences," Rodionov had said.
"If extreme measures are not taken to reform the army in the near future, the consequences for the state could be catastrophic."

Rodionov has played down talk of a military rebellion but said repeatedly that problems, which have included acute shortages in equipment and supplies and wage delays, could soon get out of control unless defence spending is increased.
